title: What awe is
hook: the feeling of something vast that you can't quite take in; every tradition names it differently

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was quarrel, a real complaint that can still be set down. Your line was let it go, and with it, sixty days on forgiveness closed.

The edge of a canyon, where the ground simply stops. A thunderstorm rolling in over a lake. A newborn's whole hand wrapped around one finger. A night sky so far from town that the stars look crowded. Some things don't fit. The mind tries to take them in and runs out of room. For some, the breath catches; for others, there's stillness, or a laugh, or tears that make no sense. Then the moment passes. For the weeks ahead, this path stays with that moment, starting with the plainest question: what is it?
screen: `THE EDGE OF A CANYON.` → `SOME THINGS DON'T FIT.` → `WHAT IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, an old word with two sides. Some readers hear the old word fear, in lines like this one, as something closer to awe. The psalm says, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom". Not terror that makes you run. More like standing very still because you've met something larger than you. Second, a scholar's name for it. Rudolf Otto, a German writer on religion, described the holy as a mystery that makes people tremble and draws them in at the same time. He used Latin for it: mysterium tremendum, a mystery that makes one tremble, and fascinans, what draws one in. Terrible and fascinating at once. Third, the strange thing about awe: it's often about what was there all along. Emerson, in his essay Nature, tries a thought experiment: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore; and preserve for many generations the remembrance of the city of God which had been shown!" And yet, he says, they come out every night, and we barely look. Fourth, the names. A psalm calls it glory. Moses is told he stands on holy ground. Jacob wakes and says he didn't know. The Qur'an calls such things signs. Each one gets its own day ahead, in its own words. Different words, one shared gesture underneath: looking up from what's in your hands to what's around you.
screen: `FEAR AND AWE, TWO SIDES.` · `TERRIBLE AND FASCINATING AT ONCE.` · `IT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.` · `MANY NAMES, ONE GESTURE.` · then, large: `LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: Lift your eyes slowly above everything you usually look at, screens, faces, tables, to the sky if you have it, or a treetop, or just the ceiling and the light coming in. For one minute, don't name what you see; let it be bigger than you, and let thoughts pass under it like birds. If you pray, the looking can be your prayer.
Mysterium tremendum. Rudolf Otto's Latin for the holy: a mystery that makes one tremble and draws one in at once. Today's word.
Your line: look up. The stars come out every night, whether anyone looks or not. One day short of a thousand.

howItsDone: People on this path often mark awe by pausing outdoors, at the sea, on a mountain or under the night sky, and by reading the passages different traditions wrote about such moments.

chat.says: Why do I feel scared and pulled in at the same time up here?
options: That's awe. Otto called the holy a mystery that makes you tremble and draws you in.
That's just fear of heights; real awe is only ever a calm, happy feeling.
That's your body warning you to leave; true wonder never feels scary at all.
